findings.title: Allegiance and jurisdiction
findings.claim: The pericope draws Iblis's jurisdictional boundary through allegiance: following him exposes a person to his threatened outcome, while the focus denies him governing authority over God's servants and names the Lord as their sufficient custodian.
findings.mechanism: In 17:63 the consequence is attached to whoever follows Iblis; 17:64 lays out ways of agitating, addressing, involving, and promising. The focus then sets those acts beside عِبَادِي, negates سُلْطَٰنٌ over them, and says the Lord is enough as وَكِيلًا. The contact between a following relation and the paired authority/custody terms makes the boundary relational rather than geographic.
findings.reader_payoff: Influence, a person's uptake, and jurisdiction become distinct relations: the campaign can reach people without giving Iblis an independent claim over those held by God.
findings.containment: The limit does not erase the attempts named in 17:64 or establish that no one can be moved. The claim concerns this pericope's contrast in allegiance and custody; it does not settle the scope of عِبَادِي in every usage.

epistemic.reason: The channel's exact focus words and the adjacent follower, influence, and unavailable-guardian context are supplied directly; the cited branch records fit those carriers.

findings.reader_payoff: The reader can hold the categorical limit together with the real campaign immediately before it: a voice and promise may solicit a response without becoming coercive rule.

findings.title: Guardianship within exposure to danger
findings.claim: The Lord named sufficient as وَكِيلًا in 17:65 is shown as the agent who guides passage, rescues, carries, and provides; the same pericope also places danger within His domain and says no alternative guardian can be found against Him. The assurance is custody, not immunity.
findings.mechanism: The focus's sufficient guardian meets 17:66's gentle propulsion of a ship, 17:67's rescue from distress, 17:68's threat and absence of any wakil against the Lord, and 17:70's carrying and provision. These actions make guardianship operational, while the hazard sequence prevents it from being read as exemption from the Lord's judgment.
findings.reader_payoff: Protection and exposure become intelligible together: Iblis lacks the rival custody denied in 17:65, while the Lord remains the agent both of rescue and of judgment.
findings.containment: The alternative remains that 17:66-70 is a separate warning about ingratitude rather than a direct exposition of 17:65. Neither reading makes the focus a promise that danger never occurs.

epistemic.reason: The context sequence and exact root-occurrence coordinates are supplied, but the before/after synthesis is from a legacy_unbound reconstructed HFT response; its contextual branch roles remain attributed.

findings.claim: The focus's supplied oil-for-light branch, met by the deceptive promise, blindness, and path imagery in 17:64 and 17:72, forms an exploratory image of false illumination: Satan's promise glitters but does not guide the servants along a visible way.
findings.mechanism: The focus word سُلْطَٰنٌ has a qualified branch for plant oil used in lighting. The separate deceptive-glitter occurrence in 17:64 meets the repeated blindness and path occurrences in 17:72; together they activate that light image by analogy and return it to the denied focus authority as a contrast with trustworthy guidance.
findings.reader_payoff: The denial gains a surprising image: the adversary's promise may shine attractively while leaving the route unseen, so its glitter cannot function as reliable illumination.
findings.containment: This is an exploratory, HFT-attributed image only. سُلْطَٰنٌ is not glossed as lamp or oil here; the ordinary authority/proof reading remains intact, and the packet's source evidence differs over the oil's precise kind and regional use.

epistemic.reason: The focus branch is independently recorded but qualified, and the cross-ayah image is a surprising legacy_unbound HFT inference rather than an ordinary lexical reading.

findings.title: Worship and aid as an external prayer frame
findings.claim: In the explicitly added Fātiḥa verse, exclusive worship and the request for help meet the focus's servants, sufficiency, and guardian terms; this overlay lets 17:65 sound as an assurance addressed to people who worship God and seek His aid.
findings.mechanism: نَعْبُدُ in 1:5 shares the focus's supplied worship/servanthood branch at عِبَادِي, while نَسْتَعِينُ names seeking aid and meets the focus's كَفَىٰ and وَكِيلًا carriers. The external prayer's voiced dependence thus changes the boundary from an abstract limit on Iblis into a relation of worship and reliance on God's sufficient guardianship.
findings.reader_payoff: The focus can be heard beside a concrete plea: those who worship God and seek His aid are met with the assurance that their Lord suffices as guardian.
findings.containment: This is an exploratory external overlay, not a claim that 17:65 is a direct answer to this exact recitation or that every use of عِبَادِي denotes precisely the first-person group of 1:5. It adds a prayer frame without replacing the native pericope reading.

epistemic.reason: The exact focus and external word occurrences are supplied and their branch contacts are explicit; the cross-surah prayer relation is an authored contextual inference, bounded to 1:5.
